title: Scammers use AI to impersonate immigration attorneys to dupe immigrants with fake legal services

reading.body:
Scammers used AI-generated video to impersonate a real, named immigration attorney across hundreds of fake social media profiles. The fabricated content showed the attorney offering specific services at a specific price, directing viewers to a WhatsApp number where fraudsters collected payments through peer-to-peer payment apps. The failure here is impersonation: generative tools were used to produce convincing likenesses of a real person without his knowledge or consent, and those likenesses were deployed at scale across multiple platforms before any platform detection caught them.

The problem surfaced not through platform moderation but through victims contacting the real attorney's office. Removal required a hired anti-piracy firm, and even then the scale reached thousands of accounts before action was taken. That sequence shows the gap between the speed at which AI-generated impersonation content can be created and distributed and the speed at which platform enforcement responds.

What is not established is who is operating the scheme, where they are located, or whether any law enforcement action has produced findings, charges, or recoveries.

reports.title: Scammers steal identity of renowned Miami attorney to target immigrants on social media
South Florida immigration attorney says AI scammers are using his identity to target immigrants
Scammers use AI to impersonate immigration attorneys to dupe immigrants with fake legal services
Legal resident loses thousands seeking citizenship to AI immigration attorney

summary:
Angel Leal, a South Florida immigration attorney with over 30 years of experience, reports that scammers are using artificial intelligence to steal his identity and defraud vulnerable immigrants. Criminals have created hundreds of fake social media profiles and AI-generated videos showing Leal offering immigration services he never provides, including US residency assistance for $2,200. The problem escalated dramatically over the past three months after potential clients began calling his office about suspicious activity. His team hired an anti-piracy company that has removed nearly 6,500 fake accounts, including 3,500 from TikTok, 2,400 from Facebook, and 544 from Instagram.

The scams typically start with social media videos directing viewers to contact a WhatsApp number, where fraudsters send phony contracts and request payment through apps like Venmo, Zelle, or Cash App. Some fake videos feature testimonials from supposed former clients praising Leal's services. Leal warns immigrants to verify anyone offering legal services online and avoid paying money upfront through digital payment apps. He plans to contact local and federal authorities this week to investigate the scams and has changed his personal phone number in response.
